You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

messages.content:
Diagnosis:
The failure in the test `testReadingOfFirstStoredEntry()` suggests that the content read from the ZIP archive is invalid (contains NUL bytes) when using commons-compress version 1.7, whereas it works correctly in version 1.6.

The test reads the first ZIP entry expecting its size to be 5 bytes and the content to be "data\n". The failure indicates that the bytes read do not match, implying an issue in how the ZIP archive input stream decodes or reads the ZIP entry content.

From the current bug report, it is clear that the problem did not exist in 1.6 but appears in 1.7, hinting at a regression or change in internal handling.

Looking at the `ZipArchiveInputStream.getNextZipEntry()` method, this method reads the local file header, parses flags, including those for UTF-8 encoding and data descriptor presence, and sets up the entry accordingly. It reads the file name, extra data, and processes ZIP64 extra data if applicable.

Specifically, if the entry uses a data descriptor (hasDataDescriptor == true), the size and compressed size are not read directly but expected to be present after the compressed data in a trailer structure.

The `readDataDescriptor()` method reads these values after finishing reading the entry data.

From looking at `closeEntry()` method, it ensures that all bytes of the current entry are read or skipped before moving to the next entry.

A possible root cause for the test failure may involve the misinterpretation or mishandling of the data descriptor or the compressed size/size fields in the local file header or the data descriptor. If the implementation incorrectly sets the compressed size or the size to zero or NUL bytes (due to, for example, a wrong or missing data descriptor read), the reading of entry content would return incorrect data.

The test ZIP file "COMPRESS-264.zip" likely uses stored entries (no compression) with a data descriptor, and if the new code incorrectly reads or ignores these data descriptors, it may result in invalid contents being read.

The difference between 1.6 and 1.7 in behavior points to a specific change in how data descriptors or entry sizes were processed.

No recent bug reports are strongly related; they address different archive formats or features.

Thus the diagnosis is:
- The regression in commons-compress 1.7 causing NUL bytes instead of actual data likely stems from incorrect reading or processing of the data descriptor for stored entries in `ZipArchiveInputStream`.
- This causes the entry size or compressed size to be set incorrectly, leading to reading wrong or padded bytes when calling `IOUtils.toByteArray(in)`.
- The problem probably lies in the reading of the data descriptor or the ZIP64 extra field processing or in the logic deciding when/how many bytes to read for stored entries with data descriptors.
- This matches the behavior seen in `readDataDescriptor` and `processZip64Extra` methods, and the call sequence in `getNextZipEntry` and `closeEntry`.

The root cause is a flawed handling of the data descriptor or ZIP64 extra fields leading to incorrect entry size, causing incorrect extraction of stored entry contents and resulting in the test failure.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
